## Overview

The Komi (*комияс*, *komijas*; also *коми-войтыр*, *komi-vojtyr*) are a Permian ethnic group indigenous to northeastern European Russia. They primarily inhabit the basins of the Vychegda, Pechora and Kama rivers, with most living in the Komi Republic and others in Perm Krai, Murmansk Oblast, Khanty–Mansi Autonomous Okrug and Nenets Autonomous Okrug. The Komi are divided principally into the northern Komi-Zyryans and southern Komi-Permyaks, with smaller groups traditionally associated with particular rivers. The 2010 census recorded 228,235 people who indicated their nationality as Komi, compared with 336,309 in 1989. Their language belongs to the Permian branch of the Uralic family. Folk culture is strongly connected with forest settlement, river-based subsistence, distinctive regional clothing, wooden architecture, mythology and cuisine.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Regional Komi clothing** — Komi national dress has numerous local variants. Regional distinctions concern embroidery technique, fabric type and ornamentation. Southern and central Komi clothing closely resembles that of Northern Russians and other Finno-Ugric groups, while the clothing of the Izhma Komi has features in common with Nenets dress.

**Izhma Komi costume** — The Izhma Komi costume is a regional form associated with the Izhma Komi, who live in sparsely wooded areas. Its documented points of distinction are its local character and its common features with Nenets clothing.

**Men’s clothing** — Men’s clothing remained comparatively similar throughout Komi-inhabited territories, apart from the winter costumes of Komi males.

**Women’s clothing** — Women’s dress shows greater regional variation than men’s clothing. Differences are expressed through embroidery, fabrics and ornamentation.

No named Komi textile patterns or specific pattern vocabulary are identified in the sources.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe Komi clothing in general and distinguish men’s and women’s dress. Men’s clothing was mostly similar across Komi territories, except for regional winter costumes. Women’s clothing varied more strongly by region, especially in embroidery technique, fabric and ornamentation. Southern and central Komi dress resembled clothing among Northern Russians and other Finno-Ugric groups, while the Izhma Komi costume shared features with Nenets clothing.

### Architecture

Komi settlements were commonly organized as large, multi-courtyard churchyards and villages built along or near rivers. Because the Komi inhabited heavily forested territories, wood was traditionally the principal material for houses and farm buildings. Komi dwellings resemble North Russian houses in their internal structure.

Two major house types are named: the **Sysol house type** (*Сысольский тип*) and the **Vym house type** (*Bымский тип*). The Sysol house is square-shaped and divided internally into a commercial section and a private section for residents. The Vym house is difficult to distinguish from the Sysol type, with its main differences found in the windows and internal arrangement. The Izhma Komi, living in sparsely wooded areas, use *chum* tents. Komi church architecture developed under the influence of Stephen of Perm’s efforts to spread Orthodoxy and included wooden churches with tented roofs, similar to constructions in Northern Russia and Pomorye.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They identify wood as the traditional material for houses and farm buildings and mention *chum* tents among the Izhma Komi, but provide no catalogue of everyday objects.

## Music & performance

The Komi language article reproduces the text of the Komi-Zyryan folk song “Катшасинъяс” (*Kačaśinjas*, meaning “Daisies”), including versions in the Anbur script, the Zyryan Cyrillic alphabet and a modern Latin alphabet.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources document the **Fish Pie Festival** (*Черинянь гаж*), held annually on the last Sunday of June in the village of Byzovaya, Pechora Raion. It is associated with the Komi fish pie known as *черинянь*.

The sources also describe older religious beliefs and Christianization. Most Komi myths concern shamanism and paganism, while the Komi were gradually Christianized through the efforts of Stephen of Perm. A specific life-cycle calendar of birth, coming-of-age, marriage and funerals is not provided. Komi mythology describes beliefs about the dead: the land of the dead was thought to lie far north of the living, beyond mountains, rivers and forests. Souls crossed the river *Syr Yu* (“River of Pitch”) by different means according to the deceased person’s sins, and the dead then climbed a slippery mountain. The sources state that Komis traditionally kept fingernail clippings so that they could be buried with them for use in the afterlife.

## Foodways

Hunting, gathering and fishing were long-standing sources of food. Komi diets prominently included meat, fish, berries and mushrooms. Meat dishes were more common among northern Komi, while berry dishes were more common in the south. In the northern reindeer-herding and hunting areas, meat was eaten daily; in the more agricultural south, fish was commonly eaten, while hogs and poultry were eaten less often.

Named foods include grain pies with fish, various porridges, *Serbanka*, sour soups and cold soups based on bread and kvass. The dumpling dish *pelmeni* is described as likely originating in Komi and Udmurt cuisine; its Komi and Udmurt name, *пельнянь* (*pel'n'an'*), means “ear bread.” Komi women bake fish pie (*черинянь*) on festive family occasions. Traditional beverages include *kvas* and *sur*, a type of ale.

## Oral tradition & literature

Komi mythology includes creation stories, spirits, witches and tales connected with the natural world. The most widespread creation myth concerns the struggle between the creator-gods En (*Ен*) and Omöl’ (*Омöль*), associated with good and evil. In the mythology article, En is described as a good creator god who takes the form of a swan, while Kul’ or Omöl’ is an evil creator god who takes the form of a grebe. A duck egg gives birth to them, and they rise from the primordial ocean to create the world.

Other named beings include Vasa, a water spirit; Olys’ or Olysya, a hearth spirit; Aika, a spirit protecting a specific place; Peludi-Aika, “Father Cornflower”; Pyvsyan’sa, master of the bath-house; Voipel’, god of the cold north wind and night; and Vörsa, spirit of the forest. Hunters offered Vörsa furs, bread and salt or tobacco in the hope of catching game. The notorious witch of Komi folklore is Yoma, or Yoma-Baba. Named mythological figures include Jirkap from Sindor, Joma and Pera.

The sources also mention tales of chudins, pagans who flee into the forests from the new Christian order. Research into pre-Christian Komi religion began among Russian ethnologists in the later half of the 19th century. A modern literary revival or preservation project is not described in the supplied sources.

## Language & religion

Komi belongs to the Permian branch of the Uralic family. The two principal regional standards are Zyrian in the Komi Republic and Permyak in the Komi-Permyak Okrug; Komi-Yazva is another regional variety. The Komi language has ten named dialects: Syktyvkardin, Lower Ežva, Central Ežva, Upper Ežva, Luz-let, Upper Sysola, Pećöra, Iźva, Vym and Udora. Komi has 17 cases and no grammatical gender.

The Old Permic script, also known as Anbur, was created by Stephen of Perm in the 14th century. Cyrillic was later used, and Komi briefly employed the Latin alphabet between 1932 and 1936. Since the 1940s, it has used a Russian-based Cyrillic alphabet with the additional letters І, і and Ӧ, ӧ.

Komi religion combines older shamanic and pagan beliefs with the effects of Christianization. The sources describe creator-gods, water and forest spirits, shamans, sorcerers and witches. Stephen of Perm became the patron saint of the Komi after his death.
